newsitem.title: USA: White House issues revitalization blueprint for DC.
newsitem.headline: White House issues revitalization blueprint for DC.

text.p: The Clinton Administration on Friday sent the U.S. Congress a detailed blueprint on how it would implement its proposed $3.9 billion, five-year revitalization plan for the District of Columbia.

But the 30-page draft document sidesteps one of the most volatile issues in the mounting debate over how to assist D.C. - whether the city will continue to get an annual multimillion dollar payment in lieu of taxes from the U.S. government for its use of D.C. property.

The draft "memorandum of understanding" is silent on the payment - currently $660 million a year. But a senior administration official said the White House continues to recommend that Congress wipe out the payment.

However, eliminating the issue from the MOU is expected to ease its final endorsement by D.C.'s 13-member council and D.C. Mayor Marion Barry, who already have had extensive input into the draft document.
"This restructuring is historic, probably necessary and heartwrenching," D.C Councilwoman Charlene Drew Jarvis said in a telephone interview.
"It's clear that it is a significant restructuring. We've asked for the federal government to be the state, and in many ways (with this proposal) it is," Jarvis added.
The administration official said the memorandum is "like a technical instruction manual for how the President's plan is put in place."

First outlined by the President on January 14, the plan would turn over payment of city pension liabilities for police, firefighters, jduges and teachers to the federal government; boost the federal share of the city's Medicaid payments; and take other steps.
Overall it would save D.C. roughly $770 million over five years.
The plan calls for creation of a new public authority that would establish a strategic plan for economic development in the city, including issuance of tax-exempt private activity bonds.
It would provide $250 million in tax incentives to encourage business investment both downtown and in distressed community, and to help businesses boost employment.

The corporation, for instance, could issue tax-exempt bonds to finance a broader range of business properties than currently permitted if the business is located in a "higher poverty area" and has a worforce of at 35 percent D.C. residents.
